Late Capitalism Series · Lesson 02 · Frankl

The Last Freedom

Three people. Three paths to meaning. One question that runs through all of them.

Elena
Teacher · Meaning through work

This is the third year I have taught the same unit. I know which jokes land. I know which students will ask questions and which ones are just waiting for the bell. I am good at this. I think I am, anyway.

But last week one of my students, a girl who never speaks, came up after class and asked me: "What is this actually for?" And I said "the exam." And she looked at me like I had confirmed something she already suspected.

For discussion
Elena is competent. She knows her subject. But the student's question unsettled her. What exactly did it unsettle?
Csikszentmihalyi · Flow
Csikszentmihalyi distinguished between performance and flow. Performance is executing a skill correctly. Flow is when the activity itself becomes the reward. You lose track of time because you and the task have become one thing. Elena is still performing well. But she may have stopped being absorbed by it.
Elena
Teacher · Meaning through work

I went home and thought about it. And I realised: I know how to teach. I am not sure I know why anymore. Not in a way I could explain to that girl without feeling dishonest.

The exam is not a reason. It is just the next thing. And I am not sure the next thing has ever been a reason for anything.

Your question
Frankl argued that the primary human drive is the search for meaning, not pleasure or performance. Is Elena describing the absence of meaning, or just a bad week?
Think of it this way: a bad week is when the lesson bombs, a student is rude, or the photocopier breaks. Elena is not having that. Everything is working. She is just not sure it is working for anything. Frankl called that the existential vacuum: not pain, but the absence of a reason for anything to matter. The student who asked "what is this for?" was not being difficult. She was asking the question Elena had stopped asking herself.
Frankl · Logotherapy
Frankl wrote: "Success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue." Meaning is not something you arrive at through work. It is what happens when your work is done in response to something larger than the work itself. The girl who asked "what is this for?" was asking Elena for a reason. Elena did not have one.
Making it concrete
What does Frankl mean by "meaning cannot be pursued"?

Think of two teachers. Both teach the same subject, the same level, the same textbook.

Teacher A
She teaches because it is her job. She does it well. Her students pass. But when a student asks "what is this for?", the only honest answer she can give is: "the exam." The work is competent, but it is not connected to anything beyond itself.
Teacher B
She teaches because she believes understanding a language changes how a person sees the world. Her students also pass. But the work feels different to her, because it is a response to something she genuinely cares about. The meaning is not in the lesson plan. It is in what the lesson plan is for.

Both teachers do the same work. The difference is not effort or skill. The difference is whether the work is connected to something larger than the work itself.

Frankl's point: you cannot sit down and decide to feel meaning. But when your work is done in response to something that matters to you, meaning shows up on its own. That is what "it must ensue" means. It is a side effect, not a destination.
Second path — suffering
Tomás
Architect · Meaning through suffering

People keep telling me he would have wanted me to keep going. I do not know how they know that. He was nine. He wanted ice cream and football and another episode before bed. He did not have opinions about what I should do with the rest of my life.

But I keep going. Not because of what he would have wanted. Because I do not know what else to do. And because stopping feels like a second loss I am not ready for.

For discussion
Tomás does not say he has found meaning in his suffering. He says he continues because stopping is worse. Is that the same thing?
Frankl · Unavoidable Suffering
Frankl was very precise about this. He never said that suffering itself produces meaning. He said that when suffering cannot be avoided, the way we choose to face it becomes meaningful in itself. Tomás is not finding meaning in the loss of his son. He is choosing to continue, and that choice, however quiet, is where the meaning lives. Frankl saw this in the concentration camps. Not every prisoner responded to the camps in the same way. But those who chose how to face each day, even in small ways, carried something different inside them.
Making it concrete
What does Frankl mean by "choosing your attitude"?

Think of two people who go through the same loss.

Person A
He stops. He stays home. He waits for the pain to pass before doing anything. It does not pass. Months later, his life is smaller than before. The loss took everything around it with it.
Person B
He also does not know why he continues. But he gets up. He goes to work. He does not enjoy it. One day, months later, he notices something has shifted. He is more patient. His work is quieter, more honest. He did not plan this. It happened because he kept showing up.

Neither person chose the loss. The difference is that Person B made a small, daily choice: to continue. He did not choose to grow. He chose to keep going, and the growth happened inside that choice.

Frankl's point: when suffering cannot be avoided, the one freedom you still have is how you respond to it. That response does not need to be dramatic or heroic. Sometimes it is just getting up and going to work. But that small act of choosing is where the meaning begins.
Tomás
Architect · Meaning through suffering

The thing I have noticed is that I draw differently now. Not better or worse. Just differently. I put things in the designs that I did not put there before. More light. More open space. I do not know if anyone notices. I notice.

Maybe that is the answer to your question. I do not know why I continue. But I know how I am continuing. And the how has changed. Something in the way I work has changed.

Your question
Tomás says "the how has changed." Frankl says the last human freedom is to choose one's attitude. Are these the same claim, or different ones?
Here is the difference. Frankl's claim is about a decision: even when everything is taken from you, you can still choose your attitude. That is active. What Tomás describes is more passive: he kept going, and something shifted without him planning it. He did not decide to draw with more light. It just happened. Frankl would probably say these are not opposites. By choosing to keep going, even without knowing why, Tomás created the space for something new to appear. The shift could only happen because he kept showing up.
Third path — love
Yara
Volunteer · Meaning through love

I am not there to fix anything. I have learned that. In the beginning I thought I was supposed to say the right thing. Now I know there is no right thing to say when someone is very ill. There is only whether you are really there or not.

Most people are not really there. They are thinking about what to say next. They are managing their own discomfort. The patients know. They can feel the difference between someone who is present and someone who is performing presence.

Simone Weil · Attention
Weil called sustained attention the highest form of human generosity. Not advice, not solutions, not comfort: simply attention. To attend to another person fully requires a kind of self-emptying: you must temporarily set aside your own reactions, your own discomfort, your own need to be helpful. What remains is the other person, as they actually are. This, Weil said, is what love looks like in practice: not a feeling, but an act of will.
Yara
Volunteer · Meaning through love

People ask me if the work is sad. It is, sometimes. But it is also the only place where I feel like I am doing exactly the right thing, in exactly the right way, at exactly the right time.

Csikszentmihalyi would probably call that flow. I call it the only time I stop thinking about myself. And I did not realise until I started doing this how much of my life I had spent thinking about myself.

Csikszentmihalyi · Flow and Self-Transcendence
Csikszentmihalyi's research found that in flow states, self-consciousness temporarily disappears. The person is not thinking about how they are doing. They are simply doing. Yara has found flow not in a skill or a task, but in attention to another person. Frankl called this self-transcendence: He believed that meaning is never found by looking inward. It is found by turning fully toward something or someone that genuinely matters.
Your question
Yara says "the only time I stop thinking about myself." Weil says attention requires self-emptying. Frankl says meaning is found by transcending the self. Are these three thinkers describing the same thing, or three different things that happen to point in the same direction?
Think of it like three people describing the same moment from different angles. Weil is looking at what Yara is doing: setting herself aside so the other person can be fully seen. Csikszentmihalyi is looking at what Yara is feeling: the disappearance of self-consciousness, the absorption, the loss of time. Frankl is looking at what Yara is oriented toward: something outside herself that genuinely matters. It is the same moment, described from three different angles. None of them is wrong.
Making it concrete
What does it mean to "transcend the self"?

Think of two people visiting a friend who is very ill.

Visitor A
She brings flowers. She asks about the treatment. She suggests doctors. She says "you look great." She leaves feeling she has been helpful. But the patient felt something else: the visitor was managing her own discomfort the whole time. She was never fully there.
Visitor B
She sits down. She does not try to fix anything. She listens. When the patient is silent, she is comfortable with the silence. She is not thinking about what to say next. She is not thinking about herself at all. The patient can feel the difference.

Both visitors care. The difference is that Visitor B has temporarily set aside her own needs: her need to be useful, her need to say the right thing, her discomfort with illness. What remains is just the other person.

This is what all three thinkers are describing. Weil calls it attention. Csikszentmihalyi calls it flow. Frankl calls it self-transcendence. The common thread: meaning appears when you stop thinking about yourself and turn fully toward something or someone that matters.
The question that runs through all three
Final dilemma — vote before discussing
Elena, Tomás, and Yara are all, in different ways, living meaningfully. But only one of them chose it consciously. Which one?

Frankl would resist the framing. He did not say meaning requires a moment of clear, deliberate choice. He said it requires responsiveness: the willingness to respond to what life is asking of you, even when you cannot put the question into words.

Elena is beginning to hear the question. Tomás is living the answer without knowing it. Yara has found the answer and is giving it, every time she shows up.

The most Franklian answer may be the last one, not because conscious choice is unimportant, but because meaning often arrives before we name it. The naming comes later, but the living comes first.

To close

“He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.”

Nietzsche, quoted by Frankl
